power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: is a preprint and has not yet been peer reviewed.
It has not been accepted for publication by any journal, and its content may change following peer review.
Readers should treat the arguments as preliminary and should not cite this work as peer-reviewed literature.
Consider a student attending a lecture in a language in which they are not fully fluent.
Smart glasses or an earpiece translate the lecturer's speech, organize the main points, and assemble notes in real time.
The student is not distracted and may understand more than they would without assistance.
Nevertheless, the object of attention has changed.
Rather than encountering the lecture primarily as an unfolding event, the student increasingly encounters a textual or spoken representation generated from it.
Voice, hesitation, gesture, spatial orientation, audience response, and the felt continuity of the room may recede even as comprehension improves.
Ambient AI therefore presents a problem that cannot be reduced to whether technology increases or decreases attention: it can sustain attention while changing what attention is directed toward.
The features that recede are not merely incidental.
Speakers' gestures can contribute to listeners' comprehension (Hostetter, 2011), and learners may rely differently on captions and audio depending on their proficiency (Li, 2025).
text.formatted: Speakers' gestures can contribute to listeners' comprehension <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Hostetter, 2011)</ref>, and learners may rely differently on captions and audio depending on their proficiency <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Li, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: A generated representation can therefore improve access to propositional content while redistributing attention away from other information through which the event is understood.

A systematic review of 83 higher-education studies documented the expansion of English-medium instruction but found that the evidence available at the time was insufficient to establish that it improved English proficiency or clearly harmed content learning (Macaro et al., 2018).
text.formatted: A systematic review of 83 higher-education studies documented the expansion of English-medium instruction but found that the evidence available at the time was insufficient to establish that it improved English proficiency or clearly harmed content learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Macaro et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Lecture comprehension is also a recurring difficulty.

In an Australian university study published in 2000, only 9% of the 174 respondents from non-English-speaking backgrounds who answered an immediate postlecture comprehension question reported understanding the lecture very well, while an alarming 22% not understanding much of its content (Mulligan & Kirkpatrick, 2000).
text.formatted: In an Australian university study published in 2000, only 9% of the 174 respondents from non-English-speaking backgrounds who answered an immediate postlecture comprehension question reported understanding the lecture very well, while an alarming 22% not understanding much of its content <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Mulligan & Kirkpatrick, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: In another study involving European English-medium programs, 42% of Norwegian respondents and 72% of German respondents had self-assessment scores indicating difficulty comprehending lectures in English; prominent difficulties included unfamiliar vocabulary and taking notes while listening (Hellekjær, 2010).
text.formatted: In another study involving European English-medium programs, 42% of Norwegian respondents and 72% of German respondents had self-assessment scores indicating difficulty comprehending lectures in English; prominent difficulties included unfamiliar vocabulary and taking notes while listening <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Hellekjær, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Given the prominence of such issues in classrooms when medium of instruction is a language students are unfamiliar with, many are now turning to technology to close the gap.

At a transnational English-medium university in China, students described using machine translation for reading and writing, many of them daily, and instructors reported students using simultaneous speech translation during class (High et al., 2025).
text.formatted: At a transnational English-medium university in China, students described using machine translation for reading and writing, many of them daily, and instructors reported students using simultaneous speech translation during class <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(High et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Ambient translation in lectures is therefore an existing practice in international and transnational education, and the psychological questions it raises are already practical ones.
The lecture example exposes a limitation in common accounts of technology and attention.
Such accounts often ask whether AI reduces attention, as though attention were a single quantity.
Research instead describes attention as a family of selection processes directed toward external and internal targets (Chun et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Research instead describes attention as a family of selection processes directed toward external and internal targets <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Chun et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The more precise questions are what becomes the object of attention, how that object is constituted, and whether the user recognizes the role of mediation in constituting it.
A learner absorbed in an accurate transcript can be highly attentive to meaning while attending less to the event from which that meaning was extracted.
Conversely, translation can make an otherwise opaque lecture available for the first time.
The same interface can therefore narrow contact with an event in one circumstance and restore it in another.
The argument has a defined scope.

The term ambient AI extends the ambient intelligence tradition in computing, which describes environments that are sensitive and responsive to people (Cook et al., 2009) and systems that are embedded, context aware, personalized, adaptive, and anticipatory (Aarts, 2004).
text.formatted: The term ambient AI extends the ambient intelligence tradition in computing, which describes environments that are sensitive and responsive to people <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cook et al., 2009)</ref> and systems that are embedded, context aware, personalized, adaptive, and anticipatory <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Aarts, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Following this tradition, ambient AI here refers to systems that sense an ongoing situation and produce assistance during it, including live captions, translation, generated notes, summaries, and wearable prompts.

Clinical ambient scribes and speech-enabled lecture translation illustrate real-time assistance, although only the former typically involves generative language models (Kanaparthy et al., 2025; Shadiev & Huang, 2020).
text.formatted: Clinical ambient scribes and speech-enabled lecture translation illustrate real-time assistance, although only the former typically involves generative language models <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Kanaparthy et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Shadiev & Huang, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Generative systems are distinctive because they can interpret, compress, organize, and explain an event while it continues.
The present analysis concerns the individual user's relation to the ongoing event and the representation produced from it.
The proposed process is experiential reconfiguration: ambient AI reorganizes present experience by redistributing attention between an event and a generated representation of it.
Reconfiguration is a neutral term, consistent with postphenomenological accounts in which technologies shape how the world appears to their users (Ihde, 1990; Verbeek, 2000 Verbeek, /2005)).
text.formatted: Reconfiguration is a neutral term, consistent with postphenomenological accounts in which technologies shape how the world appears to their users <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Ihde, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Verbeek, 2000</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Verbeek, /2005))</ref>.

text.text: It may scaffold contact when the representation makes otherwise inaccessible aspects of the event available, support concurrent augmentation when event and representation remain jointly relevant, or produce representational substitution when the generated output becomes the primary attentional object.
None of these relations can be inferred from task performance alone.

The central construct is therefore meta-awareness of mediated attention: awareness that a technological representation is shaping what one attends to and which features of the event are being selected, transformed, foregrounded, or omitted.
Several features distinguish ambient generative AI from older forms of mediation such as slides, handouts, and conventional transcripts.
Its output is generated during the event and may interpret, select, and compress content rather than reproduce it.
It can be private and personalized, so co-present people neither share the same representation nor see what it omits.
It is fallible in ways that may be difficult to detect because language models can produce fluent claims unsupported by the source (Ji et al., 2023).
text.formatted: It is fallible in ways that may be difficult to detect because language models can produce fluent claims unsupported by the source <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Ji et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: It is also conversational and available on demand, inviting repeated consultation while the event continues.
These features do not inevitably produce substitution, but they increase the importance of recognizing the output as a selective representation rather than as the event itself.

This paper develops a relational model of that recognition, distinguishes it from neighboring constructs, reviews relevant evidence, identifies boundary conditions, and advances propositions for future research.
Meta-awareness refers to explicit awareness of one's current experience or mental activity rather than experience alone (Schooler, 2002).
text.formatted: Meta-awareness refers to explicit awareness of one's current experience or mental activity rather than experience alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Schooler, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: In AI-mediated situations, the relevant object of meta-awareness is not only where attention has gone but also how a technological representation is organizing that attention.

Meta-awareness of mediated attention is defined here as awareness that an interface is shaping the user's attentional relation to an ongoing event, including awareness of attention moving between the event and its representation and recognition that the representation is selective.
The construct is episode specific: a user may recognize mediation in one situation yet fail to recognize it in another.
Meta-awareness of mediated attention is distinct from attentional breadth.
An event includes semantic content, but it is not exhausted by that content.
A lecture also has pace, prosody, gesture, interpersonal cues, bodily responses, interruptions, and a social and physical setting.
These features need not all occupy focal attention, and broad attention is not inherently preferable to narrow attention.
Attentional breadth describes which features of the event the user encounters; meta-awareness describes whether the user recognizes that an interface is shaping that encounter.
A student may knowingly prioritize an accurate transcript and remain meta-aware despite attending narrowly.
Another may alternate between the transcript and lecturer without recognizing that the text has become the practical center of the lecture.
The construct therefore concerns recognition of mediation, not an ideal of comprehensive awareness.
Meta-awareness must also be separated from regulation.

Recognizing that attention has moved toward a representation creates an opportunity to continue, alternate, verify, redirect, or disengage, but it does not determine which response the user will choose.
A user may knowingly remain with generated notes because semantic comprehension is the immediate priority.
Conversely, awareness may not support redirection when the display is difficult to dismiss or the underlying event remains inaccessible.
Mindfulness research helps explain this distinction by treating attention, monitoring, and regulation as related but separable processes.
In Bishop et al.'s (2004) account, mindfulness involves both the self-regulation of attention and an orientation of openness and curiosity toward present experience.
text.formatted: In <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bishop et al.'s (2004)</ref> account, mindfulness involves both the self-regulation of attention and an orientation of openness and curiosity toward present experience.

text.text: Focused-attention practice likewise depends on monitoring whether attention remains with the intended object, detecting movement elsewhere, and redirecting it when appropriate (Lutz et al., 2008). Dunne et al. (2019) further characterize mindful meta-awareness as an ongoing capacity to monitor attention and affect while attention remains directed toward an explicit object.
text.formatted: Focused-attention practice likewise depends on monitoring whether attention remains with the intended object, detecting movement elsewhere, and redirecting it when appropriate <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Lutz et al., 2008)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Dunne et al. (2019)</ref> further characterize mindful meta-awareness as an ongoing capacity to monitor attention and affect while attention remains directed toward an explicit object.

text.text: Applied to ambient AI, these accounts suggest that users may remain engaged with a generated representation while also recognizing that it has become the primary attentional object.
Such recognition is not equivalent to redirecting attention: regulation additionally depends on whether the user regards the shift as inconsistent with their purpose and has the capacity to respond.
Decentering offers a complementary explanation.

It describes a change in one's relationship to mental content through meta-awareness, reduced identification with internal experience, and reduced reactivity to thought content (Bernstein et al., 2015 (Bernstein et al., , 2019)).
text.formatted: It describes a change in one's relationship to mental content through meta-awareness, reduced identification with internal experience, and reduced reactivity to thought content <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bernstein et al., 2015</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bernstein et al., , 2019))</ref>.

text.text: Thoughts and feelings can consequently be experienced as events or representations rather than accepted unreflectively as direct reflections of reality.
In an AI-mediated episode, an analogous shift would involve encountering a transcript, summary, or recommendation as a selective construction rather than as a transparent substitute for the event.
Decentering may therefore help explain how users can remain engaged with AI output while preserving awareness of its representational status and limitations.
This application extends a construct developed primarily for relating to internal mental events and should not be assumed to transfer unchanged to technological representations.

Meta-awareness of mediated attention is accordingly proposed as a distinct construct whose relationships with mindfulness, decentering, attentional monitoring, and metacognitive control require empirical evaluation. ongoing event, and attention is distributed between the event and that representation.
The resulting relation may scaffold contact, sustain concurrent augmentation, or produce representational substitution.
User, task, event, and system conditions shape this relation, but the framework does not treat any preliminary list of conditions as exhaustive.
Meta-awareness concerns whether users recognize the distribution and the representation's selectivity; regulation concerns what they are able and willing to do with that recognition.
The attentional relation shapes outcomes directly, and regulation can in turn alter that relation, so a configuration may shift within a single episode.
Note.
Shaping conditions are intentionally stated at a general level.

Their relevance and specification may change as the construct develops; the model requires only that they be identified as theoretically justified boundary conditions rather than treated as a closed checklist.
Solid arrows indicate proposed influences, and the dashed arrow indicates monitoring.
The path from regulatory response to the attentional relation indicates that configurations can shift within a single episode.
The model separates five elements that are often conflated.

Mediation produces a representation; attention is distributed between that representation and the event; meta-awareness concerns recognition of this distribution and of the representation's selectivity; regulation concerns the user's response; and outcomes concern what is learned, remembered, noticed, or done.

This separation prevents semantic success from being treated as evidence that the event remained the primary attentional object, and it prevents awareness from being treated as evidence that regulation occurred.
The three relational configurations are analytic positions rather than rigid categories.
Experiential scaffolding occurs when mediation increases attainable contact with an event.
Concurrent augmentation occurs when event and representation remain jointly significant and the user alternates between or integrates them.
Representational substitution occurs when the representation becomes the principal attentional object and the event is encountered chiefly as its source.
A single system may support different configurations across users, tasks, and moments.
Table 1 summarizes these configurations and their illustrative conditions and consequences.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">1</ref> summarizes these configurations and their illustrative conditions and consequences.

text.text: Experiential scaffolding The representation increases attainable contact with the event and may help the user return attention to it.
Relevant event information is otherwise inaccessible or difficult to process; assistance fits the user's purpose and can be consulted without becoming compulsory.
Improved access, comprehension, participation, or contact with relevant contextual cues.
The event and representation remain jointly significant, and the user alternates between or integrates them.
Both streams contribute relevant information, and the user can coordinate them without either becoming a sufficient substitute for the other.
Complementary information and reduced processing demands, with possible costs from integration or divided attention.
The representation becomes the principal attentional object, and the event is encountered chiefly as its source.
The output repeatedly reformats an already accessible event, demands monitoring, or is treated as a sufficient account of what occurred.
Efficient access to represented content alongside reduced contact with relevant features that the representation omits.
Note.
The configurations describe relations among a user, an event, and an AI representation rather than fixed device categories.
The listed conditions are illustrative candidates for theoretical development, not an exhaustive or permanent operational checklist.
Meta-awareness and regulation should be assessed separately from semantic and contextual outcomes.
Cognitive offloading involves using bodily action or external tools to alter a task's information-processing requirements and reduce cognitive demand (Risko & Gilbert, 2016).
text.formatted: Cognitive offloading involves using bodily action or external tools to alter a task's information-processing requirements and reduce cognitive demand <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Risko & Gilbert, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: A student may offload transcription to a recording device, organization to a language model, or retrieval to a searchable archive.
Offloading can weaken encoding when the user no longer performs operations needed for learning, but it can also release capacity for interpretation, questioning, or participation.
Both outcomes are documented.

Participants who offloaded information during a copying task performed faster but remembered less of what they had copied (Grinschgl et al., 2021), whereas saving a file containing a word list before studying a second list improved recall of the second list (Storm & Stone, 2015).

text.text: The saving benefit was not observed when saving was unreliable or when the first list contained only two words.
Cognitive offloading concerns how processing demands are distributed across internal processes, bodily action, and external resources.
Its broader framework also addresses metacognitive evaluations and the allocation of resources released by automation, including consequences for situation awareness (Risko & Gilbert, 2016).
text.formatted: Its broader framework also addresses metacognitive evaluations and the allocation of resources released by automation, including consequences for situation awareness <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Risko & Gilbert, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The present account focuses more specifically on which aspects of an event or its representation occupy awareness and whether users recognize the representation's selective role.
Experiential reconfiguration focuses on this relation between the event, its representation, and awareness.
A student can refrain from offloading and still experience displacement.
Consider a learner who reads every generated caption, checks the AI's organization of the lecture, and actively relates each point to prior knowledge.
The learner remains cognitively engaged and may expend more effort than a student who simply listens.
Yet attention may be organized around the generated representation.
Conversely, a student may offload note production to an ambient system and use the released capacity to watch the lecturer, notice uncertainty in an explanation, and participate more fully.
Studies of ambient scribes report improved clinician engagement and anecdotal accounts of renewed connection with patients (Kanaparthy et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Studies of ambient scribes report improved clinician engagement and anecdotal accounts of renewed connection with patients <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Kanaparthy et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These examples illustrate why the extent of offloading need not determine the quality of experiential contact.
Divided attention is also an incomplete description.
Multiple-resource theory predicts greater interference when concurrent tasks compete for the same resources, which can include a shared sensory modality or processing code (Wickens, 2008).
text.formatted: Multiple-resource theory predicts greater interference when concurrent tasks compete for the same resources, which can include a shared sensory modality or processing code <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Wickens, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Instructional research reports comparable costs when learners must integrate spatially separated sources of information (Kalyuga et al., 1999).
text.formatted: Instructional research reports comparable costs when learners must integrate spatially separated sources of information <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Kalyuga et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: It does not distinguish an unrelated message from a live translation that carries the lecturer's meaning.
Both may draw the eyes away from the lecturer, but the first interrupts the event whereas the second mediates access to it.

Text on screen also attracts the eyes with little regard to need: viewers spend considerable time reading subtitles even when they understand the language of the soundtrack (d' Ydewalle et al., 1991).
text.formatted: Text on screen also attracts the eyes with little regard to need: viewers spend considerable time reading subtitles even when they understand the language of the soundtrack (d' <ref type="bibr">Ydewalle et al., 1991)</ref>.

text.text: The relevant question is relational: does the secondary stream return the user to the event, operate alongside it, or become the event for practical purposes?
Three further literatures describe neighboring phenomena.

Presence research defines presence as a perceptual illusion of nonmediation, in which users respond as though a medium were absent even though they can identify it when asked (Lombard & Ditton, 1997).
text.formatted: Presence research defines presence as a perceptual illusion of nonmediation, in which users respond as though a medium were absent even though they can identify it when asked <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Lombard & Ditton, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Research on aviation displays describes attentional tunneling as persisting with an information source, hypothesis, or goal at the expense of other relevant demands.

Across simulator studies, pilots using synthetic vision with trajectory guidance more often missed unexpected hazards visible only outside the display than pilots using synthetic vision alone (Wickens & Alexander, 2009).
text.formatted: Across simulator studies, pilots using synthetic vision with trajectory guidance more often missed unexpected hazards visible only outside the display than pilots using synthetic vision alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Wickens & Alexander, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: This provides a perceptual analogy for smart glasses that overlay captions or summaries.
Media multitasking research examines associations between habitual use of multiple media streams and cognitive performance, including attentional control.
However, findings vary across studies, and the direction of causation remains unresolved (Ophir et al., 2009; Uncapher & Wagner, 2018).
text.formatted: However, findings vary across studies, and the direction of causation remains unresolved <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Ophir et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Uncapher & Wagner, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The present model differs from these constructs in its unit of analysis and its separation of processes.
Presence concerns responding as though mediation were absent, whereas experiential reconfiguration can occur when the interface is fully visible but its selective role is no longer salient.

Attentional tunneling describes persistence with a source or goal at the expense of other demands, whereas the present model distinguishes whether a representation supplies access to the event, operates alongside it, or becomes its practical substitute.
Media multitasking typically concerns concurrent media use and performance across tasks; the present account concerns an episode in which one stream represents the event that another stream presents.

Its distinctive contribution is to explain how semantic engagement can remain strong or improve while contact with nonrepresented features changes, and to treat recognition of that mediation and regulation of attention as separate processes.
The most informative evidence does not yet come from ambient generative AI.
Phototaking experiments provide a stronger test of the underlying attentional proposition because they examine what happens when people mediate an experience while it occurs.
The results do not support a uniform impairment account.
They show selective changes in visual attention and enjoyment (Diehl et al., 2016), and in what is remembered (Barasch et al., 2017; Henkel, 2014).
text.formatted: They show selective changes in visual attention and enjoyment <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Diehl et al., 2016)</ref>, and in what is remembered <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Barasch et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Henkel, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Henkel (2014) led participants through a museum and instructed them to observe some objects and photograph others.
Photographing an entire object was followed by poorer memory for the object, its details, and its location than observation alone.
When participants zoomed in on a specific feature, however, the impairment disappeared, including for details outside the zoomed region.
The finding is often cited as evidence for offloading to the camera.

The zoom condition complicates that explanation, and later work points the same way. Soares and Storm (2018) found poorer memory for visual details of photographed paintings than for those only observed, even when participants used an ephemeral photo application or immediately deleted each photograph.
text.formatted: The zoom condition complicates that explanation, and later work points the same way. <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Soares and Storm (2018)</ref> found poorer memory for visual details of photographed paintings than for those only observed, even when participants used an ephemeral photo application or immediately deleted each photograph.

text.text: These findings challenge an explanation based solely on consciously relying on the camera to remember.

They are consistent with disrupted engagement or encoding, but the study did not isolate that mechanism and could not rule out automatic offloading. Barasch et al. (2017) showed more directly that mediation changes the distribution of attention.
text.formatted: They are consistent with disrupted engagement or encoding, but the study did not isolate that mechanism and could not rule out automatic offloading. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Barasch et al. (2017)</ref> showed more directly that mediation changes the distribution of attention.

text.text: Across a field study and three laboratory studies, participants permitted to take photographs later recognized more visual information and less auditory information than participants who did not take photographs.
They did not review the images before testing, and mentally taking photographs produced a similar pattern.
The effect was therefore not simply reliance on an external archive or the motor act of operating a camera.
Photo-taking oriented attention toward visually representable aspects of the scene and away from sound.
A separate series of nine experiments found that photo-taking often increased enjoyment because it increased engagement with photographable aspects of positive experiences (Diehl et al., 2016).
text.formatted: A separate series of nine experiments found that photo-taking often increased enjoyment because it increased engagement with photographable aspects of positive experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Diehl et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The benefit was weaker when the activity was already highly engaging or when taking photographs interfered with participation.
Eye-tracking in a museum showed greater visual attention to objects that participants might photograph.
These results challenge the familiar claim that mediation necessarily removes people from experience.
It can intensify contact with selected features while reducing the relative availability of others.
This literature is analogical rather than direct evidence about AI.
A camera does not translate, summarize, or converse.

The experiments nevertheless establish a principle that is directly relevant: an aid can improve engagement with the information it privileges without preserving the experiential profile of the unmediated event.
Across these studies, photo-taking improved memory in one channel and impaired it in another (Barasch et al., 2017), while also increasing enjoyment under suitable conditions (Diehl et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Across these studies, photo-taking improved memory in one channel and impaired it in another <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Barasch et al., 2017)</ref>, while also increasing enjoyment under suitable conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Diehl et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: A study that measures only one of these outcomes can produce an unduly simple conclusion.
Evidence from captions and translation first establishes that mediation can change the route through which an event becomes accessible.
When learners cannot process speech fluently, text may cease to function as a secondary aid and become their principal route to the content.
Li (2025), for example, found that lower-proficiency learners relied more heavily on captions than higher-proficiency learners, whose processing depended more on audio.
The significance of this finding is not simply that proficiency predicts caption use.

It shows that the relation between event and representation depends on baseline access: the same caption stream may scaffold one learner's contact with the lecture while remaining supplementary or redundant for another.
Once a representation becomes a major route to content, attentional redistribution does not necessarily appear as poorer learning.

Subtitle formats altered participants' gaze patterns in Liao et al. ( 2020), yet recall did not differ significantly across conditions, and bilingual subtitles were associated with lower reported cognitive load than the no-subtitle condition.
text.formatted: Subtitle formats altered participants' gaze patterns in Liao et al. ( <ref type="formula">2020</ref>), yet recall did not differ significantly across conditions, and bilingual subtitles were associated with lower reported cognitive load than the no-subtitle condition.

text.text: This pattern supports the distinction between performance and attentional relation.
Assistance may make meaning easier to obtain while simultaneously reorganizing how the audiovisual event is encountered.
A stable recall score therefore cannot establish that mediation left the experiential route to learning unchanged.
Translation further clarifies why redistribution should not automatically be interpreted as displacement.

In Shadiev and Huang's (2020) study, access to translated text was associated with lower reported cognitive load than listening to foreign-language lectures without support, as well as higher scores on two proprietary indices, labeled "attention" and "meditation," generated by a single-sensor brainwave headset (NeuroSky MindWave).
Translated text also produced higher scores on both indices than same-language English transcription, suggesting that the benefit was not simply a consequence of displaying text.
The "meditation" index was intended to reflect relaxation and should not be interpreted as a measure of meditation practice, mindfulness, or meta-awareness.
The brief lectures, partly random, partly matched group allocation, and devicederived indices limit what can be concluded about learning or awareness.

Nevertheless, the study illustrates the accessibility side of the framework: when the spoken event is not sufficiently attainable, directing attention toward a translation may restore contact with the lecture's meaning rather than displace an otherwise accessible experience.

Together, the caption and translation findings suggest that attentional redistribution must be interpreted relative to what the user could access without assistance, not against an idealized unmediated baseline.
AI-supported note-taking extends the argument because the representation no longer merely reproduces speech; it interprets the event by selecting, organizing, and connecting ideas.

This additional transformation makes the user's relation to the output especially consequential. Pi et al. (2026) found that learners who participated in note production, either independently or with AI, acquired more knowledge than learners who received AI-produced notes alone.
text.formatted: This additional transformation makes the user's relation to the output especially consequential. <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Pi et al. (2026)</ref> found that learners who participated in note production, either independently or with AI, acquired more knowledge than learners who received AI-produced notes alone.

text.text: Learners in the learner-AI condition also produced higher-quality, although less complete, notes and directed more visual attention toward the note area.

These results do not show that AI collaboration preserved contact with the instructional event, but they indicate that learning outcomes and attentional distribution vary with how the learner participates in constructing the representation.
The theoretically important contrast is therefore not between AI and non-AI note-taking as fixed media, but between different relations to the representational layer.
Note-taking research distinguishes the cognitive process of generating notes from the external product available for review (Kiewra, 1985).
text.formatted: Note-taking research distinguishes the cognitive process of generating notes from the external product available for review <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Kiewra, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: A finished AI summary supplies a product while removing much of the selection and organization normally performed by the learner.

By contrast, editing, extending, or questioning AI-generated notes can preserve constructive engagement (Fiorella & Mayer, 2016), and contingent learner-AI exchange may support the interactive engagement described by the interactive, constructive, active, and passive (ICAP) framework, which orders these modes of engagement from highest to lowest expected learning (Chi & Wylie, 2014).
text.formatted: By contrast, editing, extending, or questioning AI-generated notes can preserve constructive engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Fiorella & Mayer, 2016)</ref>, and contingent learner-AI exchange may support the interactive engagement described by the interactive, constructive, active, and passive (ICAP) framework, which orders these modes of engagement from highest to lowest expected learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Chi & Wylie, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Yet greater engagement with the representation is not equivalent to greater contact with the event.
The representation may function as a means of returning to the lecture or become the destination of attention in its own right.
This relational interpretation also avoids attributing attentional quality to a medium by default.

Claims that longhand note-taking necessarily produces deeper learning than laptop use were weakened when a preregistered replication reproduced differences in note quantity and verbatim overlap but not the original immediate conceptual advantage for longhand (Mueller & Oppenheimer, 2014; Urry et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Claims that longhand note-taking necessarily produces deeper learning than laptop use were weakened when a preregistered replication reproduced differences in note quantity and verbatim overlap but not the original immediate conceptual advantage for longhand <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Mueller & Oppenheimer, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Urry et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The broader lesson is that neither the technology label nor a learning score identifies the user's attentional relation.

Across captions, translation, and note-taking, the evidence supports a consistent conclusion: mediated support can improve access or learning while changing the route through which the event is encountered, but existing studies rarely establish whether users recognize that change.
Meta-awareness of mediated attention adds explanatory value by addressing precisely this unresolved question.
A theory of displacement that treats all representations as losses would be conceptually weak and practically exclusionary.

For a learner who cannot hear the lecturer clearly, cannot process the language at conversational speed, or cannot sustain conventional note-taking, captions, translation, and generated notes may create access rather than dilute it.

A review of more than 100 empirical studies concluded that captions improve comprehension of, attention to, and memory for video for hearing viewers as well as deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers (Gernsbacher, 2015).
text.formatted: A review of more than 100 empirical studies concluded that captions improve comprehension of, attention to, and memory for video for hearing viewers as well as deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Gernsbacher, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Research on deaf students in interpreted classrooms also documents substantially different patterns of visual attention allocation across interpreters, instructors, and displays, although it does not establish that those patterns cause differences in learning (Marschark et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Research on deaf students in interpreted classrooms also documents substantially different patterns of visual attention allocation across interpreters, instructors, and displays, although it does not establish that those patterns cause differences in learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Marschark et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: The appropriate baseline is therefore the user's attainable experience without the aid, not an imagined fully accessible unmediated event.
Without assistance, a person may devote most available capacity to decoding fragments; with it, they may recover the argument, anticipate transitions, and redirect attention to the speaker.
Lectures are already mediated by microphones, slides, language, and the lecturer's framing, so the relevant comparison is among forms of mediation and their consequences.
Evaluations should also incorporate the accounts of deaf, hard-of-hearing, and second-language users themselves rather than infer their experience from comparisons with hearing or fluent peers.
Outside education, ambient AI scribes provide a useful counterexample to the assumption that mediation displaces contact.
These systems listen during clinical consultations and draft documentation so that clinicians need not divide attention between the patient and the electronic record.
A rapid review found only six eligible real-world studies through 2024; most were observational, small, or survey based.
Reported benefits included reduced documentation burden and improved clinician engagement, but objective measures of patient-clinician attention were scarce (Kanaparthy et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Reported benefits included reduced documentation burden and improved clinician engagement, but objective measures of patient-clinician attention were scarce <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Kanaparthy et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The evidence is too weak to establish restored contact.
It nevertheless illustrates a plausible design route by which offloading can increase direct contact with an ongoing interaction.
The boundary between scaffolding and displacement turns on function, fit, and control.
Assistance is more likely to scaffold when it supplies information the user could not otherwise obtain, arrives at moments chosen or anticipated by the user, and remains easy to set aside.
It is more likely to displace when it continuously reformats an already accessible event, demands monitoring, or presents its output as a sufficient account of what occurred.
Automation research identifies a further risk: under competing task demands, people may monitor consistently reliable automation inadequately and fail to detect its errors.
Trust may contribute to this pattern, although its relationship with monitoring has not been firmly established (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010).
text.formatted: Trust may contribute to this pattern, although its relationship with monitoring has not been firmly established <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Accuracy alone does not resolve the issue.
A perfectly accurate transcript can still narrow attention to what can be transcribed.
Greater experiential breadth is not always desirable.
A student may reasonably prioritize conceptual understanding over awareness of room ambience, and a surgeon may need a narrowed attentional field during a critical procedure.
The framework does not prescribe indiscriminate openness or treat unmediated experience as inherently superior.

Its normative claim is more limited: users should be able to recognize when an interface is selecting on their behalf, understand that the representation is partial, and regulate their relation to it when regulation is relevant and feasible.
The model is intended to guide a program of research rather than prescribe a single experimental protocol.
Its claims can be evaluated in lectures, consultations, meetings, conversations, and other situations in which AI represents an event while it unfolds.

The following propositions state the principal expectations of the framework shown in Figure 1 while leaving their operational expression open to theoretical refinement and to the demands of particular settings.
text.formatted: The following propositions state the principal expectations of the framework shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> while leaving their operational expression open to theoretical refinement and to the demands of particular settings.

text.text: Proposition 1: Representational orientation.
As an AI representation becomes more continuous, salient, or interpretively complete, attention will be more likely to become organized around the representation rather than the event it represents.
Proposition 2: Conditional scaffolding.
AI mediation will be more likely to scaffold contact when it makes relevant aspects of an event attainable that the user could not otherwise access or process effectively.
Proposition 3: Conditional substitution.

AI mediation will be more likely to produce representational substitution when the representation repeatedly reformats an already accessible event, demands continued monitoring, or is treated as a sufficient account of what is occurring.
Proposition 4: Outcome dissociation.
Representation-focused attention may improve access to semantic content while reducing attention to, or later memory for, relevant features that the representation does not preserve.
The direction and value of this dissociation will depend on the user's goals and on the significance of the omitted features.
Proposition 5: Meta-awareness and calibration.
Greater meta-awareness of mediated attention will be associated with more accurate recognition of where attention was directed and of the representation's selective role.
This proposition concerns calibration rather than a presumed preference for broader attention.
Proposition 6: Regulation as a separate mechanism.
Meta-awareness will reduce unwanted displacement only when users also have the intention, opportunity, and capacity to regulate attention.
Awareness may therefore coexist with representational substitution when remaining with the representation is deliberate or when returning to the event is not feasible.
Research should also examine variation rather than seek a single average effect of "AI use."
The same support may scaffold one user, augment another, and substitute for the event for a third.
Relations may also shift within a single episode as difficulty, fatigue, goals, or trust change.
Perceptual load and expertise reversal provide useful starting points for explaining such variation (Kalyuga, 2007; Lavie, 2005), but the framework should remain open to additional moderators.
text.formatted: Perceptual load and expertise reversal provide useful starting points for explaining such variation <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Kalyuga, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Lavie, 2005)</ref>, but the framework should remain open to additional moderators.

text.text: The theoretically important task is to explain transitions in the user's relation to the event, not to classify a device as inherently beneficial, harmful, attentive, or distracting.
A more useful design goal than minimal AI is recoverable contact with the event.

Interfaces can support that goal by allowing users to reduce output density, postpone summaries, request clarification selectively, and review organized notes after the event rather than continuously during it.

Published guidelines for human-AI interaction make similar recommendations, asking systems to time services to the user's context and to support efficient dismissal of unwanted services (Amershi et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Published guidelines for human-AI interaction make similar recommendations, asking systems to time services to the user's context and to support efficient dismissal of unwanted services <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Amershi et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Translation may need to remain live, but it can be timed and positioned to reduce unnecessary competition with faces, demonstrations, or other relevant cues.
Systems should also communicate their selectivity.
A generated outline is an interpretation, not a transparent copy of the lecture.
Research on trust in automation suggests that interfaces should communicate system capabilities and reliability so that users can calibrate trust and reliance (Lee & See, 2004).
text.formatted: Research on trust in automation suggests that interfaces should communicate system capabilities and reliability so that users can calibrate trust and reliance <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Lee & See, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Communicating uncertainty, preserving links to the relevant moment, and allowing rapid return to the original speech can help prevent the summary from becoming the sole record of what happened.
User control must include the option to stop monitoring the AI without losing later access to its output.
User practice and interface design should be considered together.

Users could be taught to recognize shifts between event and representation, to verify generated interpretations against their source, and to decide deliberately when the representation should remain primary.
Such practices require direct evaluation and should not substitute for responsible design.

If a system repeatedly makes its output the most salient object, advising users simply to monitor themselves places the burden of managing mediation on the individual while leaving the interface unchanged.
Ambient AI changes experience not only by adding information or reducing effort, but also by reorganizing the relation between a user and an unfolding event.

Its output may open an event that would otherwise remain inaccessible, remain alongside the event as a complementary attentional object, or become the principal object through which the event is encountered.
These possibilities cannot be distinguished by task performance alone.

Improved comprehension may coexist with diminished contact with features that the representation does not preserve, just as narrowed attention may be fully appropriate when it serves the user's purposes.
The central theoretical issue is therefore not whether mediation is present, or whether attention has increased or decreased, but whether the user recognizes how mediation is shaping attention.
Meta-awareness of mediated attention identifies this capacity without assuming that recognition will produce redirection.
Awareness creates the possibility of deliberate regulation; intention, opportunity, and control determine whether regulation occurs.
This separation allows the framework to acknowledge accessibility and performance gains while still asking what has been selected, transformed, or omitted.
These distinctions are offered as theoretical claims, and the propositions advanced here are intended to make them open to empirical test.
On this account, ambient AI should be judged neither by the amount of assistance it provides nor by an ideal of unmediated contact.
It should be judged by the attentional relation it creates and by whether that relation remains recognizable and governable.
Assistance supports experience when it expands attainable contact with an event or serves as a representation the user can knowingly integrate, consult, and set aside.
It displaces experience when the representation silently becomes sufficient for the event and its selectivity disappears from awareness.

The decisive human capacity is therefore not resistance to mediation, but the ability to know when one is attending through AI, to understand that the resulting account is partial, and to determine whether that form of attention remains aligned with one's purposes.
Well-designed systems can support that capacity by communicating their selectivity and keeping the event recoverable.
